title: Does Language Immersion Work Without Moving Abroad? (July 2026)
summary: Wondering why language immersion works? Learn how to replicate it at home with a proven daily stack—no relocation needed. July 2026, ISSEN.
body_text: There's a version of language immersion learning that requires booking a flight, and there's a version that doesn't. The research is pretty clear on which part actually drives the gains: the quality of contact you have with the language, not the passport stamps. If you're stuck at the same intermediate ceiling and wondering why more input isn't moving the needle, the answer is probably what's missing from your daily routine, and the fix is simpler than you'd think. TLDR: Real immersion requires interactive, contextualized, and continuous contact with a language. Background audio and subtitled films don't qualify because they demand nothing from you. Moving abroad produces gains only through quality of interaction with speakers, not time spent in-country; a 2024 meta-analysis of 42 studies confirmed outcomes tracked engagement, not geography. Passive immersion (podcasts, films) builds recognition; active immersion (speaking under real-time pressure) builds retrieval. Swain's Output Hypothesis explains why years of input can still leave you freezing mid-sentence. A workable home-immersion stack combines device language-switching, target-language media on topics you care about, daily spoken output with a partner who responds, and low-stakes nightly writing. ISSEN is an AI voice tutor that supplies the active-output layer of that stack across 60+ languages, with adaptive difficulty tied to Krashen's i+1 and SRS flashcards drawn from your own conversation history. What language immersion learning actually means Immersion, in the strict sense, is continuous and meaningful contact with a target language across the ordinary business of your day. You read, listen, speak, argue, joke, and think in the language you are learning, and the language does real work for you. It carries information you actually need. That definition rules out a lot of what gets sold as immersion. Spanish radio playing while you scroll your phone is background noise. A French film with English subtitles is entertainment with a soundtrack. Neither puts pressure on you to understand or respond. Authentic immersion has three properties working at once (and most immersive language learning apps only partially deliver them): Interactive. You have to produce language, not just receive it, which forces you to notice the gaps between what you want to say and what you can say. Contextualized. Words arrive attached to situations, faces, and consequences, so meaning sticks without conscious memorization. Continuous. It happens across hours and days, building the automaticity that short bursts never reach. Why immersion produces results faster than classroom study Classroom study loads you with rules; immersion loads you with reps under real cognitive pressure, and the second is what rewires how you process the language. Stephen Krashen's input hypothesis argues that acquisition happens when learners meet language a step beyond their current level (i+1) in a context where they care about the meaning. Grammar drills rarely satisfy that condition. Real conversation at the edge of your ability almost always does. The evidence backs this up. A 2024 meta-analysis of study abroad covering 42 studies and 283 effect sizes found medium-to-large gains, with results tracking the quality of target-language interaction learners actually had, not time in country alone. Patricia Kuhl's work sharpens the mechanism. American nine-month-olds exposed to live Mandarin speakers during play picked up Mandarin sound contrasts, while babies given the same content via DVD or audio showed no measurable gain. The social loop activates learning systems passive media leaves cold. Why moving abroad is neither required nor sufficient Moving to Madrid does not automatically teach you Spanish. Plenty of expats live years abroad, order the same three things at the corner cafe, work in English, and plateau at survival phrases. The plane ticket buys geography, and geography alone is inert. What produces gains is what you do inside it: how often you initiate conversations, who you spend evenings with, whether you push through the awkward first thirty seconds of every exchange. The Tseng meta-analysis makes this concrete. Study-abroad outcomes tracked the quality of contact with native speakers, not the length of the stay. Students who clustered inside expat friend groups improved little more than peers who never left home. The corollary is the useful part. If behaviors drive the gains, you can reproduce those behaviors from your kitchen in Chicago or your apartment in Warsaw. Passive vs active immersion: understanding the difference Passive immersion means input you take in without responding: podcasts on your walk, a Spanish novel over coffee, a Turkish drama with target-language subtitles. Active immersion means production under real-time pressure: answering a question, explaining a decision, arguing a point when the other side will not wait for you to look up a verb. The two build different subskills, and confusing them is why plenty of learners follow a news broadcast fine but freeze when a barista asks a follow-up. Recognition strengthens through exposure. Production strengthens through retrieval, a separate cognitive act with its own failure modes. That asymmetry is what drives speaking fluency plateaus at the intermediate level. Mode What it trains Typical inputs Where it falls short Passive Listening comprehension, vocabulary recognition, prosody Podcasts, films, novels, native media No retrieval under time pressure Active Retrieval, grammar automaticity, pronunciation control Conversation, debate, spoken drills Needs a partner who responds in real time A working plan uses both. Passive input feeds raw material into your head; active output forces your brain to pull it back out on demand. Skip the second half and comprehension keeps climbing while speaking stays stuck at the same intermediate ceiling. How to build immersion at home without moving abroad The move that separates people who progress from people who dabble is treating immersion as a layered daily habit, not a weekend project. You stack small changes until the target language fills most of your waking hours, then make sure some of that presence demands a response from you. A workable stack: Switch your phone, laptop, and streaming defaults to the target language. Settings menus become free vocabulary drills. Replace one podcast in your rotation with a target-language equivalent at your comprehension level. Pick a topic you already care about so listening pays off in content too. Add active output daily. A ten-minute conversation with an AI voice tutor, an italki lesson twice a week, a Tandem exchange partner. Something has to respond to you. Journal five sentences at night about your day. Errors are fine; the point is retrieval under low stakes. Join one online community where your target language is the working language. Lurk first, then post. In practice, two hours of engaged output and context-rich input across a week tends to produce more gains than fifteen hours of half-attended background audio. Build the stack once, then protect it like a workout schedule. Why output is the missing piece in most immersion plans Merrill Swain landed on the Output Hypothesis by watching Canadian French immersion students who had spent years soaked in comprehensible input still produce inaccurate spoken French. Input alone was not converting into grammatical control. What was missing was the act of producing language under conversational pressure, which forces learners to notice the gap between what they mean and what they can actually assemble in real time. You can read Swain's original paper for the full argument. This explains a common frustration. You binge target-language YouTube for a year, understand most of it, then freeze the first time someone asks a question. Comprehension trained; retrieval did not. A 2024 AI chatbot speaking practice review reported gains in self-efficacy, motivation, and oral outcomes, which is what you would expect when output pressure gets cheap enough to happen daily. ISSEN: real-time voice immersion for learners who can't relocate The behaviors that make immersion work are ones a real-time voice tutor can supply on demand: unpredictable conversation, adaptive difficulty, and repetition tied to real context. ISSEN is an AI voice tutor built around that loop, delivering active immersion in 60+ languages through spoken conversation without a plane ticket or a per-session fee. A few mechanics worth naming: Vocabulary, sentence complexity, and speaking pace adjust to your level inside a single turn, holding Krashen's i+1 as a continuous condition instead of a one-time placement setting. Conversation-anchored SRS flashcards pull review items from your own session history, so each card carries the sentence you used the word in. Background mode runs from the lock screen, turning walks and commutes into hands-free spoken output reps. At $20 to $29 USD per month for unlimited practice, cost-per-rep sits far below per-session pricing on italki or Preply, where an hour with a human tutor runs $20 to $40. Human tutors still earn their place for cultural pragmatics and fossilized errors that need targeted intervention. ISSEN sits alongside them as the daily active-output layer between those sessions. The 10-minute free trial is the entry point. Open the app, pick a topic, and you are in a live conversation inside 30 seconds. Final thoughts on the immersion approach to learning a language The gap most learners hit, where reading feels fine but speaking freezes, comes down to skipping output. Build a stack that demands production every day, and that ceiling breaks. Your kitchen in Chicago or your apartment in Warsaw works just as well as Madrid once your habits do. Consider where that habit leads over the next two to three years. Mateus is a software engineer in São Paulo who started daily 10-minute voice sessions six months ago, working through Portuguese-to-English business conversation. His tutor adapts to the topics he's actually dealing with at work: project handoffs, async standup updates, performance reviews. It surfaces SRS cards drawn from his own session history. He's not working through a fixed curriculum; the practice shapes itself around what he has to do next week. That kind of continuity, where every session knows where the last one left off and what's coming up, is already available today and will only become more precise as session memory deepens. The gap between knowing a language and being able to use it under pressure is a retrieval problem, and daily spoken output is how you close it. Start a free 10-minute session with ISSEN and add real conversational pressure to your routine today. FAQ What is immersion language learning, and does it require moving abroad? Immersion language learning means continuous, meaningful contact with a target language across your daily life: reading, listening, speaking, and thinking in that language in contexts where it does real work for you. Moving abroad can create those conditions, but research shows that outcomes track the quality of native-speaker interaction you have, not your geography. A learner in Chicago who builds a layered daily practice of active output and context-rich input can progress faster than an expat who orders the same three things at the corner cafe in Spanish. Why do immersion learners who watch hours of target-language content still freeze when someone speaks to them? Passive exposure trains recognition; it does not train retrieval. Watching Spanish-language content builds listening comprehension, but when a native speaker asks you a question, your brain has to pull language out under time pressure. That is a separate cognitive act that passive media never drills. Merrill Swain's Output Hypothesis explains the gap: producing language under conversational pressure forces you to notice what you cannot yet assemble in real time, which is the mechanism that converts passive knowledge into active fluency. How does ISSEN deliver immersion in language learning without a conversation partner or travel? ISSEN functions as an on-demand AI voice tutor that supplies the behaviors immersion research actually ties to gains: unpredictable conversation, adaptive difficulty, and real-time response in 60+ languages. Vocabulary, pace, and sentence complexity adjust to your level inside a single turn, holding Krashen's i+1 as a continuous condition instead of a one-time placement setting, and background mode turns walks and commutes into hands-free spoken output reps. It fills the active-output gap that passive immersion tools (podcasts, films, reading) structurally cannot close on their own. ISSEN vs italki and Preply for daily immersion practice: which makes more sense? For learners who need daily speaking reps, the per-session pricing on italki and Preply makes consistent practice expensive: a human tutor runs $20 to $40 USD per hour, so five sessions a week is not realistic for most people. ISSEN at $20 to $29 USD per month gives you unlimited daily conversation, making it the practical layer for building speaking volume, while human tutors on those platforms remain worth scheduling periodically for cultural pragmatics and fossilized errors that benefit from targeted human intervention. How do I actually do immersion language learning at home without full-time exposure? The move that separates steady progress from stagnation is treating immersion as a stacked daily habit, not a weekend project. Switch your phone and streaming defaults to the target language, replace one podcast in your rotation with a target-language equivalent on a topic you already care about, add at least ten minutes of active spoken output daily through a voice tutor or exchange partner, and journal five sentences each night to force low-stakes retrieval. Two hours of engaged output plus context-rich input across a week produces more acquisition than fifteen hours of half-attended background audio, because the benefits of immersion language learning depend on the quality of contact, not the quantity of ambient noise.

title: What to Do With a $2 Million Inheritance
summary: Did you just receive a sizable inheritance? What you do with it will depend on a number of factors, including how you received it. Here's what to know.
body_text: Your first instinct after inheriting $2 million may be to invest. But one of the biggest financial decisions comes before you buy your first stock or fund. Get your tax strategy wrong, and you could lose a significant portion of your inheritance before investing a single dollar. First, Know How Your Inheritance Gets Taxed Before deciding what to do with your inheritance , identify exactly what you received. Different assets are taxed differently, and treating everything as one $2 million inheritance can lead to unnecessary taxes. The table below compares the tax treatment of four common inherited assets. Inherited Asset Tax Treatment Cash Generally no immediate federal income tax. Taxable brokerage account Usually receives a stepped-up cost basis, which can reduce or eliminate capital gains tax on appreciation during the original owner’s lifetime. Inherited traditional IRA Withdrawals are generally taxed as ordinary income and may be subject to IRS distribution rules. Real estate Usually receives a stepped-up cost basis, which can reduce capital gains tax if you later sell the property. A financial advisor can help you understand how each inherited asset fits into your overall tax strategy before you invest. This Tax Mistake That Can Cost You Most Once you know what you inherited, the next decision is how and when to access those assets. The timing of a withdrawal can have just as much impact as the investment itself. For example, suppose your inheritance includes a $1.2 million taxable brokerage account holding investments your parents purchased for $400,000, along with an $800,000 inherited traditional IRA. Although both accounts hold investments, they follow very different tax rules. The brokerage account generally receives a stepped-up cost basis, meaning your basis is adjusted to the fair market value of the investment at the date of death. If you sold the investments shortly after inheriting them, you generally would not owe capital gains tax on the $800,000 of appreciation that occurred during your parent’s lifetime. The inherited IRA is different. Suppose you already have $100,000 of taxable income before taking any distributions. Withdrawing the entire $800,000 IRA balance in one year would increase your taxable income to $900,000. For tax year 2026, the additional IRA income would be taxed as follows: 1 22% on $5,700 = $1,254 24% on $96,075 = $23,058 32% on $54,450 = $17,424 35% on $384,375 = $134,531 37% on $259,400 = $95,978 In this example, your estimated additional federal tax would add up to $272,245 before deductions, credits and state taxes. Most non-spouse beneficiaries, however, generally have up to 10 years to distribute inherited IRA assets. Spreading withdrawals over that period instead of taking the entire balance in one year could substantially reduce your overall tax bill. Click Your State to Get Matched With Financial Advisors That Serve Your Area Choose your state and answer some questions to get matched with up to three fiduciary advisors that serve your area. Now, Create a Plan to Invest Your Inheritance Once you’ve accounted for taxes, you can begin deciding how to invest the inheritance. The right strategy depends on when you’ll need the money and the role you want it to play in your overall financial plan . Start by setting aside enough cash to cover taxes, unexpected expenses and other short-term needs. Having that cushion can help you avoid selling long-term investments earlier than planned. Next, think about how you’ll use the inheritance. If you’ll rely on it for income within the next several years, a more conservative allocation may be appropriate. If your goal is long-term growth and you won’t need the money for decades, a larger allocation to stocks may make more sense. Your investment strategy should reflect more than the size of the inheritance. It should account for the tax treatment of each inherited asset, the investments you already own and the financial goals you’re trying to achieve. A financial advisor can coordinate both taxes and investment planning , helping protect your inheritance before positioning it to grow. title: Do Food Trucks Need a Kitchen Display System? A Practical Guide
summary: Learn when a food truck KDS improves speed and accuracy, when a printer is enough, what features to compare, and how to test the return.
body_text: Disclosure: Avocado builds point-of-sale and kitchen display tools for food trucks and restaurants. This guide explains when a KDS is useful, when a printer may be enough, and what to evaluate before choosing either option. Short answer: not every food truck needs a kitchen display system. A small operation with one order taker, one cook, and a short menu may work perfectly well with printed tickets. A food truck KDS becomes valuable when orders arrive from several channels, tickets are getting lost or misread, multiple people share the line, or the team needs better timing and performance data. The right question is not “Is a screen better than paper?” It is “Where does our current order process break down during a rush?” Your answer will tell you whether a KDS would solve a real operational problem or simply add another device to a small kitchen. What is a kitchen display system? A kitchen display system, commonly called a KDS, is a screen that receives orders from your point-of-sale system and organizes them for the kitchen. Instead of relying only on a printed ticket, cooks see active orders in a digital queue. Depending on the system, a KDS may let your team: View new orders as soon as they are submitted See modifiers, customer notes, and item quantities Sort tickets by order time or service channel Mark individual items or entire orders complete Track how long each ticket has been open Route different items to different preparation stations Coordinate dine-in, pickup, QR, and online orders For a food truck, the KDS is usually mounted where the cook can read it without blocking the prep line. The best setup keeps the screen visible, reachable, protected from heat and grease, and connected to the same order flow as the POS. Seven signs your food truck may need a KDS 1. Tickets get lost, damaged, or prepared out of order Paper tickets are simple, but food trucks are not gentle environments. Tickets can fall, curl, become greasy, or disappear beneath containers. During a rush, cooks may grab the easiest ticket instead of the oldest one. A KDS maintains one visible queue and can make aging tickets easier to spot. 2. Your team regularly misses modifiers “No onions,” “extra sauce,” and allergy-related notes can be easy to overlook when a printer uses small type or a ticket is folded. A well-designed KDS gives modifiers consistent placement and stronger visual emphasis. It does not replace employee training, but it can reduce the opportunity for mistakes. 3. Orders arrive from more than one channel A truck may take orders at the window, from a handheld, through QR codes, and through an online ordering page. If each channel creates a separate workflow, the kitchen has to mentally merge several queues. A KDS connected to all channels can put those orders in one sequence. 4. More than one person works the line Paper can work well when one cook owns every ticket. It becomes harder when a grill cook, fryer cook, and expediter need to coordinate. A KDS can give the whole team the same view of what is waiting, what is being prepared, and what is ready. 5. Customers frequently ask where their order is If the front counter cannot tell whether an order is waiting, cooking, or ready, employees interrupt the kitchen to ask. A connected order workflow can provide clearer status information and reduce those interruptions. 6. Rushes feel chaotic even when sales are strong A line at the window is a good problem only if the kitchen can process it predictably. When the team relies on shouting, memory, and stacks of paper, adding volume can quickly create remakes and refunds. A KDS will not increase cooking capacity by itself, but it can make the existing capacity easier to manage. 7. You want usable ticket-time data A printer tells you what was ordered. A KDS can also record when the kitchen received and completed the order. That data can help identify slow menu items, understaffed periods, and unrealistic pickup estimates. When a kitchen printer is still the better choice A KDS is not automatically an upgrade for every truck. Paper may be the better option when: Your menu is short and rarely uses modifiers One employee takes and prepares most orders You handle a low, predictable number of tickets Your team strongly prefers physical tickets You have limited wall space or no safe mounting location Your current printer workflow produces very few errors A printer is also an excellent backup. Some operators use a KDS as the primary workflow and keep a kitchen printer available for outages, catering orders, or unusually detailed tickets. Food truck KDS versus kitchen printer Visibility A KDS keeps all active orders in a single queue and can highlight older tickets. Paper is easy to hold and move, but the team must physically organize it. Reliability A printer has fewer software dependencies, although it still needs power, paper, and a working POS connection. A KDS depends on its device, application, network configuration, and POS integration. Ask every vendor exactly what happens if internet service drops. Modifiers and long orders A KDS can use color and layout to make modifiers more noticeable. Paper remains useful for long catering orders or workflows where cooks need to attach a ticket to packaging. Performance data A KDS may capture ticket times and completion activity. A printer generally does not know when an order was completed. Space and maintenance A mounted screen saves counter space but needs a secure location away from direct heat, steam, and impacts. A printer needs counter or shelf space, replacement paper, and periodic cleaning. What a food truck should look for in a KDS Clear modifier formatting Ask for a live demonstration using your actual menu. A generic demo order will not reveal how the screen handles nested modifiers, combo meals, substitutions, or allergy notes. Offline behavior Food trucks often work in locations with inconsistent connectivity. Confirm whether local POS orders continue reaching the KDS during an internet outage, what happens to online orders, and how the system resynchronizes afterward. Order-channel labels The kitchen should be able to distinguish a window order from an online pickup or QR order. That context helps employees choose the right packaging and handoff process. Simple controls A cook wearing gloves should not have to navigate a complicated interface. Common actions such as bumping, recalling, and viewing an order should be obvious and require few taps. Readable hardware Evaluate screen size, brightness, viewing angle, mount quality, and touch responsiveness. A consumer tablet may be inexpensive, but it must still survive vibration, grease, heat, and daily cleaning. POS integration The fewer systems employees have to reconcile, the better. Confirm that menu changes, modifiers, refunds, canceled items, and multiple order sources behave consistently between the POS and KDS. Our broader guide to the best POS systems for food trucks covers the rest of the buying decision. Support during service hours Ask who answers when the screen stops receiving orders during a Saturday rush. Find out whether support is included, what hours it operates, and whether the vendor can diagnose the POS, network, and KDS together. How much does a food truck KDS cost? The total cost may include the display device, mount, KDS software, installation, networking equipment, and support. Some POS providers include KDS functionality in a plan, while others charge per screen or location. Do not evaluate the KDS fee in isolation. Ask for an itemized quote that includes: Upfront hardware and mounting costs Monthly or annual KDS software fees POS plan requirements Installation and menu-configuration fees Replacement and warranty terms Payment-processing requirements Support fees and contract length The return is operational rather than automatic. A KDS is valuable if it prevents enough remakes, reduces enough ticket delays, or helps the same team handle more orders. Measure those problems before buying so you have a baseline for comparison. A simple way to test whether a KDS will pay off Track the number of weekly remakes caused by missed items or modifiers. Estimate the food, labor, refund, and customer-recovery cost of each remake. Record typical ticket times during normal periods and peak periods. Count how often employees stop cooking to find, clarify, or reorder tickets. Compare those costs with the complete monthly KDS expense. Run the test for at least two representative weeks. If ticket confusion is rare, keep the printer and invest elsewhere. If the same problems appear every rush, a KDS deserves a serious trial. How to introduce a KDS without disrupting service Clean up the menu first. Remove duplicate items and standardize modifier names before sending them to a new screen. Choose the mounting location. Confirm visibility, reach, power, airflow, heat exposure, and cable routing. Test every order channel. Submit window, handheld, QR, and online orders with modifiers and cancellations. Define ownership. Decide who bumps completed tickets and who recalls an order when something is missing. Run paper and screen together. Keep printing tickets during the first few services while employees learn the new workflow. Review the data. Compare ticket times, errors, and employee feedback with your baseline. Before signing a contract, use these essential questions for choosing a POS system to evaluate the full platform, not only the kitchen screen. Frequently asked questions Can a food truck KDS work without internet? It depends on the provider and network design. Some systems can continue routing local POS orders over the truck’s local network while internet service is unavailable. Online orders and cloud-dependent functions may behave differently. Request a live offline demonstration before buying. Should a food truck use both a KDS and a printer? Many trucks benefit from a hybrid setup. The KDS can manage the active queue while a printer provides backup tickets, packaging labels, or copies for complex orders. How many KDS screens does a food truck need? Most small trucks should begin with one well-positioned screen. A second screen makes sense only when separate stations have distinct responsibilities and enough volume to justify independent queues. Will a KDS make the kitchen faster? A KDS can reduce time spent sorting, searching for, and clarifying orders. It cannot fix an overcomplicated menu, inadequate equipment, poor prep, or insufficient staffing. Treat it as a workflow tool rather than a substitute for kitchen fundamentals. What screen size is best for a food truck? The correct size depends on viewing distance, available wall space, and how much order detail must be visible. Test the device inside the truck rather than choosing from a specification sheet. The bottom line A food truck needs a KDS when the cost of order confusion is greater than the cost and complexity of the screen. If your printer workflow is dependable, keep it. If modifiers are missed, channels are fragmented, or rushes become difficult to coordinate, a connected KDS can give the kitchen a clearer source of truth. Avocado combines food-service POS and kitchen display workflows with setup and ongoing support. Book a demo to test the workflow using your menu and service model.

Como uma empresa que depende de seus parceiros de canal para ajudar a impulsionar nosso negócio na América Latina, nosso sucesso está intrinsecamente ligado ao sucesso de nossos parceiros. Aqui estão alguns destaques dessa conversa, juntamente com minha perspectiva sobre como continuaremos a vencer, juntos. O caminho para uma maior rentabilidade Durante anos, construímos uma base sólida em verticais principais como o varejo. Embora isso continua sendo uma parte vital do nosso negócio, acreditamos que o verdadeiro crescimento e a rentabilidade para nossos parceiros estão na expansão do nosso alcance coletivo. Devemos olhar para novas oportunidades em manufatura, transporte e logística, saúde e comércio eletrônico. Essas indústrias enfrentam uma pressão imensa para se modernizarem, e elas precisam da expertise que nossos parceiros fornecem, respaldada pelo portfólio de tecnologia líder da indústria. Desde a Zebra continuamos a fazer investimentos significativos em nosso portfólio para ajudar nossos parceiros a capturar essas oportunidades. Elas permitem que os clientes digitalizem seus ambientes e automatizem suas operações com insights em tempo real. Colocando uma linha de frente conectada à prova Muitas vezes falamos sobre como as nossas soluções digitalizam e automatizam os fluxos de trabalho, mas como isso se reflete na prática? Essas implementações podem realmente transformar o balanço financeiro? A resposta é um sim rotundo. Trabalhamos com a Oxford Economics para medir esse impacto e os números falam por si só. Imagine se os 20 principais varejistas da lista Forbes Global 2000 decidissem otimizar profundamente seus fluxos de trabalho. O resultado? Um salto médio de 3 bilhões de dólares em receita e 110 milhões de dólares extras em lucros para cada marca. De fato, as evidências do último ano já nos mostram que refinar esses processos é o motor definitivo do crescimento, alcançando melhorias nos lucros de até 1,8 ponto percentual. As empresas estão vivendo uma revolução silenciosa. Dos gigantes do varejo aos líderes do e-commerce , todos estão redesenhando radicalmente sua forma de operar. A fórmula vencedora já não é um segredo: consiste em fundir o poder da Inteligência Artificial, da automação e da análise de dados com o talento e a intuição humana. Ao construir esse núcleo de operações hiperinteligentes, as marcas não estão apenas disparando sua rentabilidade, mas também levando a experiência e a satisfação do cliente a um nível completamente novo. Nosso plano para o sucesso: Execução e parceria A região da América Latina demonstrou anos consecutivos de crescimento notável. Esse resultado não decorre de um único produto ou iniciativa, mas de um compromisso com uma estratégia compartilhada. Nós ouvimos nossos parceiros, Investimos nas pessoas certas e também no portfólio mais sinérgico de soluções. Nossa visão se concentra em tornar as operações de linha de frente em todo lugar digitalizadas, automatizadas e inteligentes. Nós projetamos o hardware, software e soluções de automação que formam a base para operações inteligentes. E são o nossos parceiros os que dão vida a isso. A experiência deles, os relacionamentos com os clientes e a capacidade de execução definem nosso sucesso coletivo. Para 2026 e além, nosso plano continua claro: trabalhar em conjunto, nos preparar diligentemente e executar sem falhas. Eu acredito em nossa capacidade compartilhada de ajudar nossos clientes a navegar em um cenário de mudanças constantes e construir um futuro competitivo mais resiliente. Os pontos acima representam apenas uma fração da conversa.
